video_title: You Ain’t Seen Nothing Yet | TCAf 267
gist: Strategas policy strategist Daniel Clifton joins The Compound and Friends two days after a Democratic midterm wave (including a Texas governor and legislature flip) to explain why the market is repricing AI/data-center capex: local and state backlash against data centers (38 of 40 ballot referendums lost, Virginia's tax hike, Texas moratorium) threatens ~10% of projects, crushing semis and data-center supply chains while hyperscalers with existing compute hold up. He frames the sell-off as a buyable midterm clearing event, flags healthcare (Medicaid managed care, life-science tools via NIH) as the policy winner, and sees lower oil/rates and a shrinking deficit as offsets, with Strait of Hormuz and drug-price headline risks.

insights.claim: In the 2026 midterms, six Senate candidates won states that the other party's presidential candidate had carried by more than 10 points two years earlier, versus only five such cases in the prior 35 years, signaling depressed Trump-base turnout, an energized Democratic base and independents swinging away.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: The scale of the wave gives Democrats real legislative leverage (budget, debt ceiling) that markets must price.
insights.quote: In 35 years, there were five Senate candidates who won a state the other president won two years before by more than 10 points. Okay. We had six of those happen Tuesday night.

insights.claim: Voters have removed the party in power in 10 of the 11 federal elections since the financial crisis, a rate of turnover not seen since Reconstruction, which Clifton attributes to trend growth falling from ~3% to ~2% and stagnant living standards.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Policy regimes are flipping every two years, so investors should not extrapolate any single administration's agenda for long.
insights.quote: the voters of this country have removed the party in power in 10 of those 11 elections.

insights.claim: Clifton estimates American households would be $5.6 trillion richer had the economy grown at 3% instead of 2% since the financial crisis, and says this income shortfall is fueling populism globally.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Slow-growth populism is a structural driver of policy volatility and anti-corporate sentiment.

insights.claim: The US effectively has four political parties (two factions in each party, e.g. MAGA vs. traditional Republicans and mainstream Democrats vs. DSA), and 2028 could be the first truly populist presidential election in a hundred years as younger voters demand different policy in both parties.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Populism on both sides raises long-run risk for big tech, pharma pricing and corporate concentration regardless of which party wins.
insights.quote: in 28 you have a real chance for the first time to have a true populist election in a hundred years in the United States

insights.claim: Contrary to the narrative, the Democrats who won Senate seats in Kansas, Iowa and South Carolina are not Bernie Sanders Democrats, so the result is partly a vote for moderation and bipartisan deal-making with Republicans up in 2028.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Unlike 2018, markets are not pricing a Medicare-for-all style threat; deals are more likely than radical legislation.
insights.quote: So, this was actually a vote for moderation. And I don't think that that's getting enough play right now.

insights.claim: Clifton's team ignored polls this cycle and relied on special-election results and early-vote data; Republicans were losing Texas districts by 35 points in specials, and Texas early vote moved 17 points toward Democrats, a leading indicator of the gubernatorial flip.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Hard voting data (specials, early vote) can front-run political outcomes better than polls or betting odds.
insights.quote: we had a no poll policy. We were not going to report on any polls because polls are garbage. We used hard data.

insights.claim: Trump lost about 20 points among non-college-educated white men, largely rural voters squeezed by diesel, fertilizer, tariffs and data centers, even though that cohort has seen the fastest decline in unemployment.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Rural input-cost pain and data-center opposition are now electorally decisive issues.

insights.claim: A CNBC All-America Economic Survey showed 36% of respondents naming government corruption as a top-two issue, ranking above groceries, gas prices and immigration; Clifton says in Republican rural Iowa voters cited Don Jr.'s crypto deals, congressional trading and prediction markets.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown / Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: A congressional stock-trading ban and scrutiny of crypto/prediction-market ties are plausible early agenda items.

insights.claim: Clifton concluded after a June trip to Iowa that fewer data centers would be built and Republicans would lose the Senate, crediting Byron Wien's practice of making people tell you what's on their mind.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: On-the-ground field work caught the data-center backlash months before the market priced it.
insights.quote: I walked out of Iowa in June and I was one trip and I was like, "We're going to build fewer data centers and the Republicans are going to lose the Senate."

themes.theme: Data-center backlash and AI capex risk

insights.claim: Of roughly 40 data-center referendums on the midterm ballot, 38 went against the industry, and in one case voters also recalled the three city commissioners who approved a Meta data center.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Local opposition is the main reason projects are cancelled and is now proven at the ballot box.
insights.quote: there were 40 referendums on the ballot on Tuesday on data centers. 38 of them went against the industry.

insights.claim: Clifton's framework is three layers of data-center risk: local opposition (cancelling most projects), state governments (which hold the most power, making governor races matter more than Congress), and a federal leg where Democrats may use the debt ceiling to strip 100% expensing of data-center capital equipment.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Loss of full expensing would directly raise after-tax cost of AI capex and is not yet discussed by the market.
insights.quote: they're going to use the debt ceiling as leverage to get Trump to take away 100% expensing of capital equipment for data centers.

insights.claim: Governor races in Ohio, Georgia and Texas covered about 40% of the data-center pipeline, and Texas was meant to absorb spillover from states restricting builds, so the Texas flip was the decisive negative.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Geographic concentration of the AI buildout makes it unusually exposed to a handful of state political outcomes.

insights.claim: Under the 'Boone Pickens rule' (nobody cares if New York bans fracking as long as Pennsylvania, Texas and Oklahoma allow it), data-center bans only matter when key states turn; that happened the third week of June when Virginia passed a $600 million data-center tax and Texas Gov. Abbott signaled action, which Clifton says is the day data-center-related stocks peaked relative to the S&P 500.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Track policy in the swing-capacity states, not the headline bans, to time AI-infrastructure trades.
insights.quote: Boon Pickins on fracking used to say nobody cares if New York bans fracking.

insights.claim: After Virginia's new governor enacted a $600 million data-center tax increase, Blackstone pulled the state's largest data-center project within two days and Amazon cancelled four already-zoned Northern Virginia data centers, effectively killing Northern Virginia construction while Richmond and Charlottesville-area builds continue.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Virginia is the template: state taxes/regulation translate quickly into cancelled capex.

insights.claim: Texas has an Abbott-imposed moratorium on data centers, an energy audit due December 10 and a public hearing December 17; the new Democratic governor, now with the legislature, plans to keep the moratorium until lawmakers pass data-center taxes and regulations during the January-June session.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Key catalyst dates (Dec 10, Dec 17, January state-of-the-state speeches, spring session) for AI infrastructure stocks.
insights.quote: I'm keeping the moratorum in place until the legislature actually comes up with taxes and regulations for the data centers.

insights.claim: Clifton's working assumption is that roughly 10% of planned data-center projects could be lost, requiring analysts to cut capex forecasts and flow that through to earnings; range of outcomes should narrow once governors give state-of-the-state speeches in January.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: A modest capex haircut can still produce large equity moves in the suppliers priced on capex growth.
insights.quote: You have to adjust your capex forecast. And if it's 10% down, you got to do that.

insights.claim: Louisiana is going the opposite way and embracing data centers (e.g. a Meta project) because projects can go behind the grid so consumers are insulated from rate increases, the state welcomes the jobs, and PR has been better; Clifton also expects Wisconsin's new governor to embrace data centers, whereas PJM-interconnected Northeast states mix data-center load into consumer rates.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Behind-the-meter/off-grid power arrangements are the policy unlock; expect capex to migrate to friendly states.

insights.claim: Clifton's April study found data centers pay a large share of local property taxes (about 40% in Loudoun County, where rates have fallen 10 years in a row), creating roughly a $20,000 home-value differential per homeowner, but the industry never ran an education campaign.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: The fiscal benefit is a lever companies can deploy to win local approvals; lack of messaging is a fixable cause of backlash.
insights.quote: 40% of my property tax is now being paid for by the data centers.

insights.claim: Opposition to data centers is largely non-economic (fears of cancer, water use, noise, loss of rural character, Terminator-style AI anxiety, job loss), so Wall Street's assumption that towns can simply be paid off is wrong.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Money-based fixes may not restore approvals, implying more durable restrictions than the consensus expects.
insights.quote: I thought I could solve this through economic issues and you start to realize the concern is none economic issues.

insights.claim: Hosts argue the market reaction is overdone because construction unions like data-center work and even a Democratic governor imposing a moratorium on new construction is unlikely to shut down existing work sites; Meta's president publicly asked a newly elected governor to meet after inauguration to keep the investment.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: In-progress projects and labor support limit downside; the sell-off may overshoot.

insights.claim: Environmental groups and hyperscaler-funded business groups are negotiating a set of environmental standards for data centers, a possible path to resolving the standoff that will take time.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: A negotiated standard could be the eventual re-rating catalyst for AI infrastructure.

insights.claim: Clifton expects Trump to respond by locating data centers on federal land (already being mapped for housing supply) to outrun the clock, since he views them as a national-security necessity to compete with China.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: A federal-land workaround would partially offset state restrictions; watch for executive actions.

themes.theme: Market reaction: semis down, hyperscalers hold

insights.claim: The day after the election the S&P 500 rose 1.7% while Nvidia and semis fell, as the market celebrated a decisive result with no contested election, court battles or capitol unrest and an expected end to the Iran war; the next day the Nasdaq 100 (QQQ) closed down 6.4% and the S&P 500 down 4.4% as capex cuts were priced.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown / Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: A rare direct line from a political outcome to a macro-scale market move, because AI dominates index weight.
insights.quote: the market is loding to the close. The Q's are down 6.4, the S&P is down 4.4.

insights.claim: Across Clifton's 45-stock AI screen, only the hyperscalers and Qualcomm were up; data-center parts suppliers (industrials, data-center real estate, Caterpillar, semi-equipment, power generation) were destroyed, which he says was the correct reaction.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: The 'picks and shovels' of the buildout carry the policy risk, not the compute owners.
insights.quote: the data center trade has always been about the parts that go into the data center.

insights.claim: Twenty of 25 stocks in a semiconductor basket fell 10% or more over two days, QQQ decoupled sharply from both MTUM and SMH, and Taiwan Semiconductor fell 9%, a stock that rarely moves that much.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick / Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Extreme correlation breaks signal forced positioning unwinds rather than orderly repricing.

insights.claim: Clifton suspects a large fund is blowing up in the crowded AI trade, likening it to July when Situational Awareness blew up and the market felt it before the name was known.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Forced liquidation can create indiscriminate selling and later opportunity in quality names.
insights.quote: Somebody's probably blowing up.

insights.claim: If compute is going to be scarcer, those already owning it (Microsoft, Amazon, Google) hold a more valuable asset, explaining why cloud hyperscalers were barely down; Google's resilience also suggests AI is less of a threat to search than feared.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Constrained supply favors incumbents with installed compute over suppliers selling into the boom.
insights.quote: if we're going to build less compute than those who have compute are sitting on something that's more valuable today than it was 2 days ago.

insights.claim: Clifton calls Meta 'a great Democratic stock' because the market worries most about Meta's free cash flow (no cloud revenue backing its spending), so restrictions that handcuff Zuckerberg's capex are cash-flow positive; Meta rose as Democratic sweep odds rose.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Capex-constrained spenders can re-rate on improved free cash flow even as suppliers fall.
insights.quote: I'm like Meta is a great Democratic stock and people look at me like I'm crazy

insights.claim: Nvidia is down 21% and in a bear market, and the 'it's only 14 times earnings' argument is fragile: after 12 months of multiple compression in Nvidia and Broadcom, a 5% cut to forward earnings could hypothetically drop the stock 40%, and the market never believed AI earnings growth would persist into 2027-28.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown / Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Low P/E on peak-cycle earnings is not a margin of safety when earnings are capex-dependent.
insights.quote: If if Nvidia's earnings are 5% lower >> over the next 12 months than we expected them the stock could fall 40%.

insights.claim: Elon Musk suffered roughly $110 billion of personal losses in two days across Tesla and SpaceX after spending $400 million on the election, as Democrats now control Starbase's state and fewer data centers are expected.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Musk-linked assets carry concentrated Texas political and data-center exposure; venture capitalists in AI (e.g. Anthropic) also face lower exit values and congressional scrutiny.

insights.claim: AI data centers are expected to drive about 75% of next year's GDP growth and perhaps 60% of expected earnings growth and dominate index weight, so a sector-level political issue becomes a macro market event.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Concentration risk means policy hits to one theme now move the whole index and the economy.

themes.theme: Midterm seasonality and the buy-the-dip case

insights.claim: The S&P 500 has not declined in the 12 months following a midterm election since 1938, with an average return of +14.8%, because markets price the worst during midterm years and the election acts as a clearing event.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Historical base rates favor buying post-midterm weakness.
insights.quote: It's always an aberration and it never breaks the pattern.

insights.claim: Midterm-year corrections tend to be sharper than other presidential-cycle years, and the deeper the intra-year decline, the bigger the subsequent rebound; Clifton cites 2010, 2018 and 2022 as examples.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Sell-off depth can be read as a contrarian signal for 12-month forward returns.

insights.claim: Across every partisan control combination over the last hundred years, stocks have been higher afterward, so which party controls Congress matters little for the broad index.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Avoid de-risking on partisan outcomes; position by sector instead.

insights.claim: Clifton compares the current indiscriminate selling to municipal bonds after the 2010 midterm, when fears of cut state aid and forced bankruptcies let investors buy tax-free California munis at 12-13% yields, which became one of the greatest trades ever.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Policy-panic sell-offs can create generational entry points, but require waiting for clarity.

insights.claim: Midterm elections are usually about sectors and sub-industries rather than macro, and in year three of a presidential cycle tech has historically been the worst-performing sector while healthcare also tends to fade.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Seasonality argues for caution on tech into 2027 and timing exits on healthcare.

themes.theme: Macro offsets: oil, rates, deficit, Fed

insights.claim: Clifton's out-of-consensus view is that the deficit likely improves next year even with a budget deal, because roughly $600-700 billion of one-off stimulus (tariff refunds after the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs, and One Big Beautiful Bill distributions) rolls off.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Fiscal tightening plus slower data-center capex raises growth risk but supports lower Treasury yields.
insights.quote: The deficit's probably going to get better here. This is a wildly out of consensus view.

insights.claim: Slower data-center buildout means less corporate debt competing with Treasuries and, combined with lower oil if the Iran conflict winds down, should bring market-driven interest rates down and fewer Fed rate increases.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick / Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Rate-sensitive sectors could benefit as an offset to AI capex weakness.

insights.claim: Clifton told clients Fed Chair Kevin Warsh should factor in fewer data centers and not raise rates as much, and expects Warsh to begin major financial deregulation within weeks (lower reserve requirements, later liquidity coverage ratio changes) so banks absorb Treasuries while the Fed shrinks its balance sheet; each $250 billion of balance-sheet reduction equals one fewer rate hike.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Bank deregulation is bullish for banks and, if inflation falls without hikes, for depressed real estate.
insights.quote: for every $250 billion balance sheet reduction we get. That's one less rate increase I got to do.

insights.claim: The Strait of Hormuz dictates every other financial asset right now; Clifton remains in the higher-for-longer oil camp because Iran's IRGC believes it can now wait Trump out and cannot accept being attacked without responding, so a deal requires the strait to stay open daily.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Market hopes for falling oil post-election may be premature; energy and rate relief are not guaranteed.
insights.quote: There was regime change in Texas before there was regime change in Tyrron.

insights.claim: Real estate meetings are described as gloomier than funerals because nothing but data centers is getting built, but non-AI reshoring (e.g. Kimberly-Clark building US factories, visible in lobbying disclosures on permitting and R&D incentives) should start showing up in construction data.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Lobbying disclosures can flag non-AI capex beneficiaries that could replace data-center construction demand.

themes.theme: Healthcare as the policy winner (with drug-price headline risk)

insights.claim: Healthcare has outperformed in 12 of the last 14 midterm election years by about 10% on average, and Clifton's January call to be bullish healthcare and staples has worked.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Seasonal and policy tailwinds support healthcare allocations through the midterm year.
insights.quote: this is the 12th midterm election year out of the last 14 where healthcare outperforms.

insights.claim: A Democratic increase in the NIH budget flows tick-for-tick into life-science tools earnings (a colleague matches daily federal spending line items to stocks), with AI-driven drug discovery as an additional tailwind; Illumina's stock has been strong despite weak earnings.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Life-science tools are a direct, measurable beneficiary of Democratic budget priorities.
insights.quote: every dollar that goes out of NIH goes right in the life science tools earnings.

insights.claim: Democrats' second priority is blocking OBBB Medicaid cuts, sending Medicaid managed-care and hospital names (Centene, Molina, HCA, THC) up about 12% after the election; a Texas Medicaid expansion under the flipped legislature would be the largest single expansion opportunity for them.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Texas Medicaid expansion is an underappreciated upside catalyst for Medicaid MCOs and hospitals.

insights.claim: Clifton predicts an ambitious Democratic healthcare bill (national health system, ~50 drug price cram-downs per year, ending the orphan-drug exclusion) will be reported around Thanksgiving and spook generalists crowded into large-cap pharma/biotech, but will never become law.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Expect a headline-driven pharma sell-off that may be a buying opportunity given low odds of passage.
insights.quote: It will be reported in the Wall Street Journal around Thanksgiving that we're going to do all this massive price control on drugs and people are going to freak out. It will never become law.

insights.claim: Clifton expects Democrats to trade Iran war funding for healthcare and renewable-energy concessions, likely yielding within about six months a global (international reference) price on Medicaid drugs, which is small for big pharma but hits companies with high Medicaid exposure like Gilead (HIV) and Vertex (cystic fibrosis); a Medicare version would be far bigger.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Medicaid-heavy drugmakers carry specific pricing risk; watch whether talks expand to Medicare.

insights.claim: Growth managers who did not want to be 80% chips and AI have rotated since roughly September into healthcare secular growth (Eli Lilly, biotech, life-science equipment, AI-related healthcare), and Scott Galloway argued GLP-1s may be a bigger societal story than AI.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Healthcare is the emerging destination for growth capital rotating out of AI hardware.

insights.claim: Clifton argues Gilead's hepatitis C cure saved Medicare hundreds of billions but drew backlash for its $80,000 price because it failed to explain the benefit in Washington, the same mistake the AI industry made with data centers.
insights.speaker: Daniel Clifton
insights.so_what: Industries that fail to lobby and message their benefits invite punitive policy.
insights.quote: if you're not at the table, you're on the menu in Washington.
